justice: Both sides of the roadway appear to have continuous sidewalks separated from traffic by curb and landscaped strips, indicating some balanced allocation of space beyond vehicles.

The corridor strongly prioritizes motor-vehicle throughput (multiple wide lanes under an elevated structure), which can limit equitable spatial resources for non-motorized users despite the presence of sidewalks.

No visible pedestrian crossings, curb ramps, or tactile paving are discernible in the scene, reducing practical accessibility for all users at intersections and for those needing barrier-free features.
safety: A central landscaped median and clear lane markings help organize traffic movements and reduce head-on conflict risk for drivers.
Sidewalks are set back from the carriageway with curbs and green buffers, lowering the likelihood of direct pedestrian–vehicle conflicts along the segment.
The long, straight, wide road geometry under an elevated viaduct can encourage higher vehicle speeds, which increases severity risk for any crossing pedestrians/cyclists where crossings occur.
livability: The environment is dominated by large-scale road and viaduct infrastructure with very limited active frontage or visible destinations, reducing street vitality for everyday use.
Few people and no visible street-level amenities (shops, kiosks, community facilities) are present, suggesting low social activity and limited everyday convenience along this segment.
Although there is greenery (trees and hedges), the overall setting reads as a transport corridor rather than a place to linger, limiting perceived livability for most road users.
sustainability: Street trees and continuous planted strips along both sides and in the median provide some ecological value (shade potential, habitat, air-quality co-benefits).
No visible public-transport stops, shelters, or transit priority features appear in the frame, limiting support for mode shift away from private vehicles in this segment.
Lack of visible cycling infrastructure (protected lanes, markings, or bikeway separation) reduces the attractiveness of low-carbon travel options.
aesthetics: The linear perspective of the viaduct and the orderly tree planting create a sense of visual structure and coherence.
The elevated concrete structure is visually heavy and dominates the streetscape, which can reduce overall visual appeal compared with human-scale streets.
Greenery is present but relatively uniform (hedges and evenly spaced trees) with limited design detail or landmark elements, resulting in a somewhat monotonous appearance.
comfort: The viaduct provides substantial overhead shade on part of the corridor, which can improve thermal comfort for users near/under it during hot conditions.
There are no visible benches, rest areas, or human-scale shelters on the sidewalks, reducing physical comfort for people who need periodic resting.

Wide vehicle lanes and the open corridor likely generate higher traffic noise and wind exposure; combined with limited enclosure at pedestrian level, this can reduce psychological comfort for walking.
walkability: Sidewalks appear continuous on both sides with a buffer of landscaping from moving traffic, supporting basic pedestrian movement along the segment.
No marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or median refuge islands are visible, making safe crossing uncertain and weakening walking network connectivity.
The corridor lacks visible destinations and frontage activity, which reduces walking attractiveness and perceived convenience for all road users who might walk for short trips.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lanes, bike symbols, or physical protection are visible; cyclists would likely need to mix with fast motor traffic or use sidewalks, both of which reduce comfort and safety.
The road appears wide and designed for higher speeds, which increases perceived danger for cycling without separation.
No bicycle parking, bike-share stations, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible, limiting end-to-end cycling usability and convenience.
